text:
Global higher education experts are urging universities to embrace artificial intelligence (AI) as a catalyst for change rather than a threat, calling for a fundamental rethink of how students are assessed.
But for high-stakes exams such as Korea's College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), where traditional testing methods are difficult to replace, they stress the need for greater investment in technology to detect AI-assisted cheating.
Korea has been gripped by growing fears of AI-assisted cheating, as concerns over the misuse of smart glasses and other wearable devices spread beyond the CSAT to university admissions, campus exams and professional licensing tests.
Kuancheng Huang, a professor at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University in Taiwan, called for greater investment in technology to detect AI-assisted cheating, particularly in high-stakes exams. Huang visited Seoul to attend the Times Higher Education Innovation & Impact Summit 2026 at Korea University.
"Just invest in technology to prevent this from happening because that's so important," Huang told The Korea Times.
Although cheating devices are becoming increasingly sophisticated, he said the technology to counter them is available, making the challenge largely a question of how much authorities are willing to spend.
While stronger detection measures may be needed for standardized exams, experts also called on universities to rethink how they evaluate students in the AI era.
Huang suggested shifting the focus from final answers to students' reasoning and problem-solving processes, arguing that traditional assessments are becoming less effective at measuring students' actual abilities as AI tools grow more sophisticated.
John Kao, president of National Tsing Hua University in Taiwan, echoed the need for a new approach, arguing that restricting emerging technologies would do little to prevent cheating.
"Cheating has been around from the beginning of time. It's just now the tools are getting more sophisticated," Kao said.
"It's not about taking away the tools, because the ones who cheat will always find tools to cheat with, but to emphasize academic ethics."
Kao said the university requires students and faculty to disclose their use of AI, comparing the practice to citing sources in academic research.
Dawn Freshwater, executive director of the Worldwide Universities Network, also urged universities to embrace AI as an inevitable part of education while ensuring students develop the critical thinking and ethical judgment needed to use it responsibly.
"We have to accept that students will be working and living in a world that is surrounded with AI, immersed in AI," she said.
She emphasized that universities must teach students to think independently and produce original work, using AI to support their ideas rather than replace them.
"Original thought augmented by AI but not driven by AI," she said.
